where: Section 1, cost paragraph and algorithm description
problem: It says the search returns -1, "which is never a valid index". In Python this is false: negative indices are legal, so a[-1] is the last item of the list. A student who forgets to test for -1 and writes a[result] silently gets the last element instead of an error, which is exactly the bug the sentence claims cannot happen.
fix: Say: it returns -1 as a "not found" signal. Real positions run from 0 to n-1, so -1 never collides with a position that was actually found. Careful: Python allows negative indexing, so a[-1] is the last item — always test the returned value against -1 before using it as an index.

problem: The answer says "-1 can never be a valid index, so it is unambiguous." As written it is wrong for Python, where -1 is a valid index (the last item). Only the point that 0 is a real position is correct.
fix: Answer: 0 is a real position (the first item), so it cannot signal failure. -1 lies outside the range 0 to n-1, so it cannot be mistaken for a found position; the caller must still check for -1 before using the result as an index, because Python reads a[-1] as the last item.

where: Section 1 and Section 2 code vs. text
problem: The text says the functions return the index or -1, but the code returns a pair (index, comparisons), and the shown output is a tuple such as (999, 1000). A student matching the prose to the run may be confused about what the function actually returns.
fix: State it once: these versions return a pair (index, comparisons); index is the position of the first match, or -1 when the target is absent. The comparison counter is added only to show the cost.

problem: The heading promises an "exchange sort", but the section teaches bubble sort and selection sort. Bubble sort is the exchange sort; selection sort is not one, so the label is loose.
fix: Retitle as "Sorting: list.sort(), sorted(), bubble sort and selection sort", or keep "exchange sort" and drop selection sort from that subsection.
